target: AG1’s claim that dissection is a valuable part of biology teaching because it builds fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, critical thinking, and hands-on learning
objection: Real-animal dissection typically relies on animals caught in the wild, and that wild capture harms local populations and biodiversity; therefore, the educational value comes at a nontrivial environmental cost.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is productive because most specimens are already deceased and fetal pigs are byproducts destined for landfills
objection: Even if some specimens are byproducts, dissection programs still typically cause biodiversity-harming wild capture through animal procurement, so the practice does add meaningful ecological harm beyond merely using already-fated carcasses.

target: AG1’s claim that school dissection mainly uses already-deceased meat-industry byproducts and therefore does not create additional wild-capture demand
objection: Most dissection animals are said to be caught in the wild, so classroom dissection typically increases demand for wild-caught animals rather than mainly relying on byproducts.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection does not meaningfully add harm because specimens are already-deceased byproducts from the meat supply
objection: If school dissection uses byproducts from slaughter and processing, it still depends on prior animal suffering and inhumane harm in the supply chain, even if it does not increase the number of animals killed.

target: AG1’s claim that using already-dead byproduct specimens means students are not participating in inhumane harm
objection: Requiring students to work with specimens sourced from slaughter and processing still makes classroom dissection dependent on inhumane animal suffering, so the practice is ethically problematic even if the animals are already dead by the time of dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is educationally justified because it uniquely develops psychomotor skills and creates motivating ‘aha moments’
objection: Requiring students to physically dismember real animals that come from an inhumane supply chain is ethically wrong, and education should not compel participation in that harm when alternatives can cover the curriculum.

target: AG1’s claim that students are not being made to participate in inhumane harm because the specimens are already dead byproducts
objection: Even if the classroom work is on already-dead specimens, the practice still depends on animals that were harmed in slaughter and processing, so students are still tied to inhumane harm through the supply chain.

target: AG1’s claim that any chemical and biohazard risks from dissection are manageable through biosafety procedures and therefore not significant
objection: Toxic preservation chemicals and biohazard waste still create environmental and health risks that classroom procedures cannot fully eliminate, especially because the waste must be transported and disposed of elsewhere.

target: AG1’s claim that regulated disposal makes dissection’s chemical and biohazard risks acceptable
objection: Even with biosafety procedures and regulated disposal, toxic substances and biohazard waste still create unavoidable environmental and health harms during handling and disposal.

target: AG1’s claim that biosafety procedures and regulated disposal make chemical and biohazard harms manageable
objection: School dissection still requires toxic preservation chemicals and biohazard waste, and those risks are not fully eliminated in normal classroom use, so the harm remains avoidable if alternatives exist.

target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection should be allowed if it provides educational benefits and does not add meaningful new harm
objection: Even if dissection has educational upsides, its animal-supply chain, chemical use, and hazardous waste create avoidable environmental and health harms, and those harms should not be imposed when synthetic models and simulations can achieve the same learning goals.

target: AG1’s claim that students should be allowed to dissect because dead byproduct specimens can be used productively
objection: Students should not be required to do a practice that depends on avoidable inhumane and environmentally damaging animal harms when alternatives can meet the learning goals.

target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is not necessary because the ethical concern is only about compulsory participation in inhumane harm
objection: Requiring real-animal dissection is ethically wrong regardless of claimed psychomotor or motivational benefits, because education should not compel students to physically dismember real animals sourced through an inhumane supply chain.

target: AG1’s claim that students should be allowed or expected to dissect animals if they are willing
objection: Even for willing students, dissection should not be expected or required when it creates avoidable chemical, biohazard, environmental, or animal-harm costs that effective alternatives can avoid.
